subject: history
title: Change and Continuity in Medicine Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll judge why medicine sometimes raced forward — and sometimes stood still.
meta_desc: GCSE History — factors of change and continuity in medicine: religion, war, science, government.
final_note: You weighed the role of religion, war, individuals, science and government in medical change.

walkthroughs.body_html:
For over 1,000 years Galen's ideas dominated.

The Church protected old learning but blocked dissection. Most people could not read. War and plague disrupted progress. Continuity, not change, defined medieval medicine.

From 1500 the printing press spread Vesalius' work fast.

The Royal Society (1660) backed experiments. Microscopes let Pasteur see germs. Wars pushed surgery forward — Pare in the 1500s, Lister in the 1860s, blood transfusion in WWI.

Government action mattered hugely in modern times.

The 1875 Public Health Act forced clean water. The 1942 Beveridge Report led to the NHS in 1948. Watson and Crick mapped DNA in 1953 — opening genetic medicine.

mcqs.q: Why was Vesalius significant in the history of medicine?
options: Vesalius invented the microscope.
His 1543 De Humani Corporis Fabrica corrected Galen's errors via human dissection and accurate illustration, founding modern anatomy though not curing disease.
Vesalius discovered the cause of disease and ended humoral theory.
Feudalism was a written constitution introduced by William in 1066.

mcqs.q: Why was the founding of the NHS controversial in 1948?
options: The NHS was supported by all parties and all doctors from the start.
The British Medical Association opposed nationalisation of doctors; Bevan made concessions allowing private practice; Conservatives feared cost and central control.
The NHS was originally only for soldiers returning from WWII.
Feudalism was a written constitution introduced by William in 1066.

mcqs.q: How did the feudal system work in Norman England?
options: Feudalism was a written constitution introduced by William in 1066.
The NHS was originally only for soldiers returning from WWII.
Feudalism meant peasants were slaves owned by the king.
The king granted land to tenants-in-chief in return for knight service; they in turn enfeoffed knights who held land in return for military service to their lord.
